chapters.title: Chapter 4: When Sustainability Fails: Default, Restructuring, and Contagion

lessons.title: How Sovereign Debt Restructuring Actually Works: Haircuts, Reprofiling, and the G20 Common Framework

body.text: A sovereign debt restructuring is rarely a single haircut number. It is a negotiated menu of maturity extensions, coupon cuts, and sometimes principal reductions, measured properly only in present-value terms, and getting from default to a signed deal usually takes years specifically because of who has to agree, and in what order.

children.text: The previous lesson traced how Sri Lanka and Zambia actually got to default, and deliberately left the restructuring process itself for here. This lesson goes inside that process: the difference between a light reprofiling and a genuine haircut, how a haircut is actually measured, why a small group of holdout creditors can block an entire deal without the right contract language, and why the G20 Common Framework, built to coordinate a new generation of official creditors, has struggled with exactly the sequencing problem that made Zambia's case take years.
Reprofiling vs Restructuring: Two Very Different Treatments

columns.label: Reprofiling
points: Extends maturities and/or lowers coupons; typically leaves the principal amount untouched
Used as a lighter, faster first step, often to buy time through an acute liquidity crunch
Delivers a smaller present-value loss to creditors than a full restructuring
Ukraine's August 2022 wartime deal with private bondholders, a two-year payment suspension, is a clean example

columns.label: Restructuring (Haircut)
points: Involves a genuine reduction in what creditors ultimately recover, whether through a face-value cut, a deep coupon cut, or both
Used when the underlying debt load is judged unsustainable even after buying time, not merely illiquid
Delivers a materially larger present-value loss, often the outcome of the multi-year Common Framework negotiations covered later in this lesson
Sri Lanka's and Zambia's eventual deals, covered in the previous lesson, both fall into this category

body.text: Ukraine's own trajectory shows both treatments applied to the same country in sequence. Its August 2022 deal with private bondholders was a reprofiling, a two-year payment freeze agreed quickly given the extraordinary wartime circumstances, with no reduction in principal. As the war continued far longer than that initial freeze anticipated, Ukraine returned to the table for a deeper restructuring in 2024, this time involving an actual reduction in the present value of what bondholders would recover. The lighter treatment bought time; it did not resolve the underlying sustainability question.

children.text: How a 'Haircut' Is Actually Measured: NPV, Not Just Principal

body.caption: CF(t) = the cash flow due in year t, y = the exit yield used to discount (the market's required return on the sovereign's post-restructuring risk), T = years to maturity
Comparing the present value of the new instrument's cash flows to the present value of what the original bond promised, at the same discount rate
A worked example: $100 face value, 10% exit yield

body.label: Implied NPV Haircut (at a 10% exit yield)
body.context: Discounting both cash flow streams at 10%: NPV(old) ≈ 95.0, NPV(new) ≈ 77.3, per $100 of face value. Notice the principal, $100, was never reduced; the entire haircut comes from the lower coupon and the extended maturity.

body.title: Compute the Haircut Yourself
body.prompt: Using NPV(old) ≈ 95.0 and NPV(new) ≈ 77.3, both per $100 of original face value, from the worked example above, and Haircut = 1 - NPV(new)/NPV(old), what is the implied NPV haircut, in percent?
body.explanation: 1 - (77.3 / 95.0) = 1 - 0.8137 ≈ 0.1863, or approximately 18.7%. This is the real economic loss to creditors, even though the bond's face value was never cut, only the coupon and the maturity date changed.

body.text: This is why governments often prefer to structure relief as a maturity extension and coupon cut rather than a face-value cut: it delivers a real, sometimes substantial, NPV haircut to creditors while allowing the government to say publicly that not a single dollar of principal was cut. The number that actually matters to a bondholder is the NPV haircut, not the headline description of the deal.

children.text: Collective Action Clauses: Solving the Holdout Problem

markDefs.definition: Standard modern sovereign bond terms allowing a specified supermajority of bondholders, typically 75%, to approve a restructuring that then legally binds every bondholder in that series, or, under 'single-limb' aggregation, across multiple series at once, preventing a small minority from refusing the deal and suing for full repayment instead.

children.text: A restructuring only works if it actually binds every creditor. Without the right contract language, a small minority of bondholders can refuse the deal, hold out for full repayment, and sue in court instead, precisely what nearly derailed Argentina's restructuring for over a decade. Modern sovereign bonds now standardly include
, specifically designed to prevent a repeat of that saga.

body.title: Argentina's Holdout Saga and Why Bond Contracts Changed

events.title: Argentina's Default
events.description: Argentina defaults on roughly $100 billion of debt, at the time the largest sovereign default in history.

events.title: Two Exchange Offers, Most Bondholders Participate
events.description: Argentina completes two debt exchanges covering roughly 93% of the defaulted bonds, offering steep haircuts that most bondholders accept rather than pursue litigation.

events.title: The Pari Passu Ruling Blocks Payments
events.description: A small group of holdout creditors, led by NML Capital, part of Elliott Management, wins a US court ruling that Argentina cannot pay the exchanged bondholders without paying holdouts the same pro-rata share, an injunction that effectively blocks Argentina from servicing its restructured debt at all.

events.title: A Blocked Payment Becomes a Credit Event
events.description: Blocked by the US court order from making a scheduled payment, Argentina is ruled to have suffered a 'failure to pay' credit event by ISDA's Determinations Committee, the same episode covered in Chapter 2, Lesson 2.

events.title: Argentina Settles With the Holdouts
events.description: Under a new government, Argentina reaches a settlement with the main holdout creditors, paying a substantial premium over the original exchange terms to finally resolve the dispute.

events.title: Standard Bond Contracts Are Rewritten
events.description: In direct response to this saga, ICMA introduces new standard collective action clauses, including 'single-limb' aggregation allowing a single cross-series vote to bind multiple bond series at once, specifically to prevent a small holdout minority from blocking a future restructuring the way NML Capital did.

children.text: Paris Club, China, and Why the G20 Common Framework Exists

For decades, official bilateral sovereign debt restructuring ran almost entirely through the Paris Club, an informal grouping of mostly Western creditor governments established in 1956, operating on a principle called comparability of treatment: every creditor, official and private, is expected to receive broadly comparable relief, so no single creditor group can free-ride on another's concessions. This worked reasonably well while Paris Club members held most official bilateral claims on distressed sovereigns. Over the 2010s, China became one of the largest bilateral lenders to emerging and low-income countries, entirely outside the Paris Club structure, alongside other non-traditional lenders like India and Saudi Arabia. Restructuring negotiations had no established forum for coordinating between these two groups of creditors, a gap the G20 Common Framework for Debt Treatments, launched in November 2020, was built specifically to close.

body.caption: How the G20 Common Framework is supposed to work

cells: The debtor country formally requests debt treatment under the Common Framework, alongside seeking an IMF-supported program
The IMF's own DSA determines the country's financing gap and the scale of debt relief needed to restore sustainability, the same DSA machinery covered in Chapter 1
Paris Club and non-Paris-Club bilateral creditors, including China, India, and Saudi Arabia where relevant, jointly negotiate terms with the debtor
4. Comparability of Treatment Extended to Private Creditors
Once official creditors agree terms, private bondholders are expected to accept broadly comparable relief, though the private negotiation runs as a largely separate track

body.text: In practice, this sequencing has repeatedly stalled the process. Private bondholders are often reluctant to finalise their own concessions until they see the official terms, since committing first risks accepting worse relief than official creditors eventually get, while some official creditors have been reluctant to finalise their side until private terms are clearer too. This circular wait was a central reason Zambia's case, covered in the previous lesson, took nearly three years to reach even the official-creditor stage.

children.text: Is the Framework Getting Faster? Chad, Zambia, Ghana Compared

body.caption: Three Common Framework cases, side by side

cells: Request: January 2021 (distressed rather than in outright default)
A relatively simple debt structure, dominated by one large commodity-trader loan, made coordination faster
The first case; every procedural question about non-Paris-Club coordination had to be worked out from scratch
Benefited from lessons learned in Zambia's and Chad's cases; still followed by a separate, further Eurobond exchange with private bondholders in 2024

body.title: Face Value vs Present Value
body.scenario: A sovereign offers bondholders a choice between Option A, a 30% cut to the face value of their bonds with the same coupon and maturity, and Option B, no change to face value but a coupon cut from 7% to 2% and a maturity extension from 5 to 12 years.
body.prompt: Without doing the full discounting, what is the one number you would need from the market before you could say which option actually costs bondholders more?
body.modelAnswer: You need the appropriate exit yield, the discount rate the market would require on the sovereign's new, post-restructuring risk profile, to convert both options into comparable present values. Option A's haircut is transparent at 30% of face value, applied immediately. Option B's cost is entirely hidden inside the coupon cut and the seven extra years of maturity extension, and depending on the exit yield used, its NPV haircut could easily be smaller than, similar to, or larger than 30%. This is exactly why a restructuring that avoids touching the headline face-value number, easier to sell politically as 'no haircut', can still deliver a real and sometimes larger loss to creditors than one that does.

body.title: Check Your Understanding
body.question: Which of the following best explains why a sovereign restructuring is sometimes structured as a maturity extension and coupon cut with no reduction in the bond's face value, rather than a straightforward haircut to principal?
options: It is legally impossible for a sovereign to reduce a bond's face value under any circumstances
It can deliver a real, sometimes substantial, NPV haircut to creditors while allowing the government to say it never cut principal, which can be politically and reputationally easier domestically
Rating agencies do not consider a maturity extension to be a credit event at all
Bondholders always prefer a maturity extension over a face-value cut, so it is the default choice in every negotiation
body.explanation: A maturity extension and coupon cut can deliver a meaningful NPV haircut, as the worked example in this lesson showed, roughly 18.7% at a 10% exit yield, without ever touching the bond's stated face value. This lets a government describe the deal as having preserved principal, which can matter politically, even though creditors are absorbing a real economic loss measured in present-value terms.

children.text: A Field Checklist for Reading Any Sovereign Restructuring

body.title: Before You Evaluate Any Sovereign Restructuring Offer
steps: Always convert the offer into an NPV haircut using a realistic exit yield; never rely on the headline face-value number alone

Check whether the bonds carry standard collective action clauses and, if so, whether they use single-limb aggregation, which determines how easily a holdout minority could block or be bound by the deal

Identify whether official bilateral creditors are involved, and if so, whether they include non-Paris-Club lenders like China, since this determines whether the G20 Common Framework's sequencing applies
Track whether the official and private creditor tracks are proceeding in parallel or whether one is stalled waiting on the other, the exact sequencing problem that delayed Zambia's case for years
Compare the country's timeline against the Chad, Zambia, and Ghana precedents to gauge whether the process is running faster or slower than the emerging norm

Check for any state-contingent or value-recovery instruments in the deal, since these can shift real recovery meaningfully depending on the country's future growth, without changing the headline haircut number

body.text: This lesson explains sovereign debt restructuring mechanics for educational purposes, using a simplified illustrative example and public reporting on real cases. It is not investment advice. Timelines, terms, and figures are approximate and change as negotiations evolve; always verify against official IMF, creditor-committee, and government statements for current details.

points: Reprofiling (maturity and coupon changes without touching principal) and restructuring (a genuine reduction in recovery) are different treatments, and a country can move from one to the other, as Ukraine did between 2022 and 2024

A haircut should always be measured in present-value terms; a restructuring that preserves face value entirely can still deliver a substantial real loss, roughly 18.7% in this lesson's worked example, once discounted at a realistic exit yield

Collective action clauses, especially single-limb aggregation adopted after Argentina's holdout saga (also covered via its CDS angle in Chapter 2), exist specifically to stop a small minority of creditors from blocking a deal the large majority has accepted

The G20 Common Framework was built to coordinate Paris Club and non-Paris-Club official creditors like China, but its sequencing, official terms first, private terms expected to follow, has repeatedly caused years-long delays

The framework does appear to be getting faster with each case, Chad, then Zambia, then Ghana, but even its fastest resolution to date took well over a year from default to an official-creditor agreement
